summary: Describes a way to attach SMPTE time-codes, the timestamps used in film and television production, to media streams sent over RTP. The method works the same way no matter which payload format the stream uses.

eli5.summary: Film crews stamp each frame with a clock reading so they can line things up later. This note shows how to attach those stamps to video and audio sent over the internet.

questions: how to send smpte time-codes over rtp
how big is an smpte time-code in rtp
subtitle: How to tag any RTP media stream with SMPTE film and TV time-codes, whatever codec it uses.

tldr.problem: Film and television production labels every frame with an SMPTE time-code, but RTP streams had no payload-independent way to carry those labels alongside the media.
tldr.mechanism: Setup parameters sent out of band describe how the time-code counts. Then mappings from RTP timestamps to time-codes travel either in a new RTCP packet type (194) or in an RTP header extension, in a compact 24-bit or full 64-bit form.
tldr.outcome: Any RTP stream can carry time-codes without changing its payload format. The cost is low bandwidth, but the RFC admits a lost RTCP packet cannot be detected.

today: RFC 5484 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2009. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Time-Codes Are Tricky
sections.content:
An SMPTE time-code counts frames and is usually displayed like a clock, hh:mm:ss.frame. When the frame rate is a whole number, such as film at 24 fps or PAL video, the time-code runs in real time.

NTSC video is the awkward case. A frame takes 1001 ticks of a 30000 tick per second clock, yet SMPTE time-codes count 30 of these frames and call that a second. The display therefore runs slow. The drop-frame format skips some frame numbers so the counter periodically catches up, which means some time-code seconds hold only 28 frames. Because neither form is an accurate clock, the RFC calls them 'time-code seconds'.

This specification carries time-codes in RTP and RTCP, associates them with a media stream and synchronizes them with the RTP timestamps. It builds on the general RTP header extension mechanism from RFC 5285.
sections.eli5: Some TV clocks run a tiny bit slower than real clocks, and some skip numbers to catch up. This note explains how to send those special clock readings along with a video.

sections.title: Design Goals and Ground Rules
sections.content:
Every RTP stream already has a media clock. If the time-code simply counts up within a 'segment' of time, the time-code at any point can be calculated from four things: the RTP timestamp at the start of the segment, the time-code at the start, the counting rate and other parameters, and the RTP timestamp you are asking about.

Two cases are considered. If time-codes are piece-wise continuous with only occasional jumps, an initial mapping plus periodic mappings in RTCP packets are enough. If continuity is uncertain, the mapping must be sent in band inside the RTP packets themselves. Both a compact and a full form of the time-code exist, because some uses need all 8 bytes of SMPTE 12M while others, such as compressed audio, care about bandwidth.

Receivers MUST support time-codes in both RTCP and RTP and both forms. Senders are free to choose. When a presentation has several streams, senders MUST keep sending the standard RTP synchronization information in RTCP even if time-codes could be used instead. Time-codes on different streams may be the same or differ, for example when they come from different source material that was edited together.
sections.eli5: If you know when a clip started and how fast the clock ticks, you can work out the clock reading at any moment. When the clock might jump around, you have to keep telling the viewer the new reading.

sections.title: Signaling the Time-Code Parameters
sections.content:
A receiver that must calculate time-codes from RTP times needs setup information, which MUST be sent out of band, for example in a SIP offer/answer exchange (RFC 3264). With SDP, the extmap attribute from RFC 5285 is used. Three values are needed:

  • frame_duration: how long one frame count lasts, in the RTP timescale.
  • frames_per_tc_second: how many frames make a time-code second, so the frame counter runs from 0 to one less than this.
  • is-NTSC-drop-frame: whether the usual drop-frame behavior applies.

The three values MUST correspond with each other; giving both duration and frame count removes any ambiguity about drop-frame counting. For a stream with a 90000 ticks per second timescale, a frame duration of 3003 and 30 frames per time-code second gives a normal NTSC time-code, while 3750 and 24 gives 24 fps film.

In SDP the three are written as frame-duration "/" frames-per-tc-second [drop], where the duration is length@rate. The URI is urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:smpte-tc. For example, a=extmap:4 urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:smpte-tc 25@600/24 suits film on a timescale of 600. The rate in the duration should match the RTP clock rate, and if the payload type changes mid-stream the extension should be repeated on the first packets of the new payload. With /drop, the first two frame numbers are omitted from each minute except minutes 00, 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50.
sections.eli5: Before the show starts, both sides agree on the rules of the clock: how long one frame lasts, how many frames make a second, and whether numbers get skipped.

sections.title: Compact and Full Time-Code Formats
sections.content:
The compact form takes 24 bits and is not binary-coded decimal. It uses fixed-width binary fields: a sign bit (1 for negative), hours in 5 bits (0 to 23, values 24 to 31 reserved), minutes in 6 bits (0 to 59, 60 to 63 reserved), seconds in 6 bits (same range) and frames in 6 bits (0 up to frames-per-tc-second minus 1). These fields are wider than SMPTE 12M's BCD layout, where only two bits hold the tens digit of the frame count, so frame numbers above 39 cannot be represented there.

The full form takes 64 bits and is exactly the SMPTE 12M layout from its Sections 7 and 8, without the 16-bit syncword. It includes units and tens of frames, seconds, minutes and hours, a drop frame flag at bit 10, a color frame flag at bit 11, and eight binary groups. The drop frame flag MUST agree with the drop indicator in the signaling. Using the color frame flag to extend the tens-of-frames field is outside the scope of this specification.
sections.eli5: There are two ways to write the clock reading: a short note with just hours, minutes, seconds and frames, or the full official form with every extra detail.

sections.title: Mappings in RTCP
sections.content:
When time-codes are piece-wise continuous, an RTCP packet gives an RTP timestamp and the time-code for the start of each run. That mapping holds for all RTP times at or after the given one, until a later RTCP packet replaces it. The RTP timestamp in the mapping need not match any frame; a change may happen part-way through a decoded audio frame, which is fine because the streams share a clock.

These packets need not use the same timestamp as the sender report in the same compound packet. They can be sent ahead of need for stored content, or just in time, for instance as early feedback packets under RFC 4585 after a discontinuity, so the client can see the mapping before the matching RTP packet is displayed.

The association is a new RTCP packet type, SMPTETC with value 194, in two forms told apart by length. The short form has length 3 (four 32-bit words) and holds the compact time-code. The full form has length 4 (five 32-bit words) and holds the full 8-byte SMPTE 12M time-code.
sections.eli5: Every so often the sender sends a little note that says: at this moment on the media clock, the time-code reads this. The receiver keeps counting from there until a new note arrives.

sections.title: Mappings in RTP and Design Trade-offs
sections.content:
When continuity is unknown, or certainty is wanted, the mapping goes in some or all RTP packets using an RTP header extension. The RFC calls this a less desirable route: some terminals find header extensions problematic, and sending the mapping in every packet uses more bandwidth. The short form is 3 bytes (24 bits) and links a compact time-code to the packet's own RTP timestamp. The long form is 12 bytes (96 bits): a full SMPTE 12M time-code followed by a signed 32-bit offset D, so a packet with timestamp T establishes the association for RTP time T+D.

To compute a time-code at time T2 from an initial code at T1, the informative implementation note suggests working zero-based: convert the initial code to a frame count, add floor((T2-T1)/frameDuration), and convert back. This avoids a 'fence post' problem with the drop-frame minutes.

The discussion section argues the design adds no new IP packets or new data to the main channel, and works with any RTP profile, payload format or encryption. Giving the time-code its own RTP stream was rejected as egregious for such a low data rate. It also admits that there is no way to detect that an RTCP packet was lost and a mapping is being used outside its intended range, and that clients should hold mappings until superseded and may need to buffer upcoming ones.
sections.eli5: If the clock might jump at any time, the sender can stick the reading right on the packets, like writing the time on every page. That is safer but uses more paper.

sections.title: Security and IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The security section is short: SMPTE time-codes are only informative and there are no known security considerations from associating them with media streams.

IANA registered the RTCP packet type SMPTETC (SMPTE time-code mapping) with value 194 in the RTCP Control Packet types sub-registry. It also registered the extension URI urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:smpte-tc in the RTP Compact Header Extensions sub-registry.
sections.eli5: Time-codes are just labels, so the authors found nothing dangerous in them. The new packet number and name were written down in the official list so nobody else uses them.
